title: Nostro vs Vostro Accounts and Why Reconciliation Breaks
summary: Learn why nostro and vostro accounts diverge, how reconciliation breaks, and how to model mirror, in-transit, and continuous exception postings line by line.
body_markdown:
Nostro and vostro accounts drift apart because your bank posts the nostro when you send the instruction, while the correspondent posts the vostro when the money settles. Banks moving money across borders reconcile the two records, and misalignments between nostro and vostro show up in that comparison. Without a line-by-line mirror nostro, reconciliation mismatches pile up in a spreadsheet until finance escalates the backlog at month-end.


This morning's camt.053 from your USD correspondent posts a $2,250,000 credit against an expected $2,500,000. The outbound wire your system released at 16:55 CET yesterday carries today's booking date. Both lines are correct at the correspondent. Neither reconciles against your mirror, and the difference sits open until month-end close.


This article walks through nostro and vostro accounts side by side, the seven ways their records diverge, and how a mirror nostro turns each mismatch into an explainable exception.


### What is a nostro account?


A nostro account is your bank's foreign-currency bank account held at a correspondent bank, in the correspondent's currency.


Banks open a nostro when they need to pay or receive in a currency where they hold no account at the central bank, and a correspondent settles cross-border movements for them.


The nostro account is the pool of funds your bank draws on to pay in that currency. The correspondent holds the balance, debits it on your instruction, and credits inbound funds back into it.


Alongside the nostro at the correspondent, your bank keeps a mirror nostro, which is an internal shadow account posted the moment an instruction goes out. The treasury sees the expected position before the statement lands.


When customer funds are pooled in an[omnibus account](https://www.formance.com/glossary/omnibus-account) at the bank instead of being held in separate customer accounts, per-customer tracking lives entirely in your internal ledger. The bank sees only the total balance.


#### How does a nostro account work day to day?


A nostro's day has four events:


1


**You send an instruction:** Your system releases a payment message (SWIFT MT103, pacs.008, or a proprietary API call) to the correspondent, and posts the movement to your mirror nostro so the expected position updates in real time.


2


**The correspondent debits or credits the nostro:** The correspondent processes the instruction against its own core, applies any queue or compliance hold, and books the entry on its cut-off schedule, which may not match yours.


3


**The correspondent returns a statement:** End of day, you receive an MT940 (legacy SWIFT) or camt.053 (ISO 20022) message listing every booked entry with its value date, booking date, and entry reference.


4


**You post your internal mirror against the statement:** Each statement line clears the corresponding mirror posting, and any unmatched line becomes a reconciliation exception with an owner and an age.


Instructed and settled movements each have their own[ledger balance](https://www.formance.com/blog/financial-operations/ledger-balance-for-product-and-engineering) , separate from the amount you can spend. Treasury needs all three states (booked, pending, and available) visible at the same time.


#### Where do nostro accounts sit on the balance sheet?


Your nostro is an asset on your books because the correspondent owes you the nostro balance on demand.


Across the two banks, the nostro asset and the matching vostro liability mirror each other. They have the same funds, booked with opposite signs on each side, so any drift between them is by definition a reconciliation break.


For a bank that holds both a nostro at another bank and a vostro for that same bank, the opposite-sign convention makes the trial balance add up to zero.


### What is a vostro account?


A vostro account is the same correspondent balance, but recorded by the correspondent. Your money is on the correspondent's books and is carried as a liability because the correspondent owes the balance back to you on demand.


A vostro account is how the correspondent holds and services another bank's funds. The correspondent debits the vostro when your instructions arrive, credits inbound payments that name your account, and posts its own fees and interest adjustments against the vostro balance.


#### How does a vostro account work day to day?


A vostro's day is the same four events as a nostro's, seen from the correspondent's side of the wire:


1


**The correspondent receives your instruction:** A SWIFT MT103, pacs.008, or API call arrives from your bank naming the vostro as the funding account, and the correspondent's core queues it for processing.


2


**The correspondent debits the vostro:** The correspondent books the debit against the vostro on its own cut-off once compliance and cover checks pass. It moves the funds out to the beneficiary or the next hop in the payment chain.


3


**The correspondent sends the statement line:** The entry lands on the MT940 or camt.053; you receive it at the end of the day, carrying the correspondent's statement ID, entry reference, value date, and booking date.


4


**You match the line against your nostro mirror:** Your reconciliation compares the statement entry to the mirror posting you made at instruction time. Any unresolved mismatch in amount, date, or reference becomes an exception.


Your mirror nostro shows what you told the correspondent to do, while the vostro shows what the correspondent did. Only the second one counts as settled, so that's the number you reconcile against.


#### Where do vostro accounts sit on the balance sheet?


The correspondent's vostro is a liability on the correspondent's books because it owes you the balance on demand.


Nostro and vostro describe one set of funds and one transaction history; the two records should match at every cut-off. If a bank runs both a nostro and a vostro with the same bank, the two accounts cancel each other out.


### Nostro vs vostro: key differences


Nostro and vostro accounts differ across seven attributes: whose books they sit on, how they're carried on the balance sheet, what currency they hold, which record counts as the source of truth, when the posting happens, entry identifiers, and how they typically break.


**Attribute** **Nostro account** **Vostro account**


Whose books the account sits on Your bank's ledger The correspondent's ledger


Balance sheet treatment Asset (the correspondent owes you the balance on demand) Liability (the correspondent owes the balance back to the account holder on demand)


Currency of the balance The correspondent's local currency (e.g., USD at a US correspondent) The correspondent's local currency (same physical balance with the same denomination)


Source of truth for a movement Mirror nostro, posted from your outgoing instruction Statement, posted from the correspondent's actual settlement


When the posting happens At instruction time, before settlement At the correspondent's cut-off, after settlement


Identifiers carried on the entry Your internal instruction ID and payment reference The correspondent's statement ID and entry reference


Typical failure mode Optimistic postings drift ahead of reality when settlement is delayed or rejected Late, corrected, or duplicated lines arrive after the day's cut-off


The two accounts describe the same money, but because the two records are written at different times with different identifiers, reconciliation is the only module where the drift becomes visible and ownable.


### Why nostro and vostro records diverge


Nostro and vostro records diverge because different systems write them at different times from different inputs.


Every unmatched statement line traces to one of several causes: cut-off timing, value date versus booking date mismatches, lifting charges taken in transit, FX rate differences, duplicate or missing statement lines, retry double-execution without idempotency keys, and mirror-account drift.


#### Cut-off timing: why late instructions book the next day


An instruction sent after the correspondent's cut-off books on the next business day, so your mirror and the statement carry different dates for the same movement.


T2, Fedwire, and other RTGS systems run different operating hours, so a payment sent before your local cut-off can still arrive at the correspondent after the correspondent's cut-off.


#### Value date vs. booking date mismatches on camt.053


Value date and booking date can differ on the same statement entry because the camt.053[usage guideline](https://www.payments.ca/sites/default/files/lynx_bank_to_customer_statement_camt.053.pdf) defines ValDt and BookgDt as separate fields on each entry.


Your mirror posts on the instructed value date. The statement line may carry a booking date one day later after a queue or compliance hold, while the statement's value date still equals your mirror's value date.


**Lifting charges under SHA and BEN**


Under the SHA and BEN charge codes, intermediary banks take fees from the principal in transit, so the statement amount is net and your posting is gross.


The charging option definitions say that under OUR the payer covers all charges, including intermediary charges. Under SHA, the payer covers the outgoing charge and the payee absorbs intermediary charges, while under BEN, the payee pays every charge.


#### FX rate differences between trade date and settlement date


In a cross-currency foreign exchange (FX) payment, the trade-date rate on the FX confirmation and the actual settlement amounts on the statement can differ from the rate used in your mirror.


The rate difference between instruction and settlement shows up as an unexplained residual against your nostro.


#### Duplicate or missing statement lines in MT940 and camt.053


A reconciliation pipeline has to handle duplicate files and late-arriving entries. A resent file may deliver every line twice, and a late booking may drop out of today's statement and roll into tomorrow's statement.


MT940 and MT950 are the end-of-day statement messages for customer and bank-to-bank accounts. Camt.053 is the ISO 20022 equivalent of MT940 and MT950.


#### Retry double-execution without idempotency keys


A timed-out instruction retried without an idempotency key risks running twice: two debits at the correspondent and one debit in your mirror.


Payment systems need idempotent execution controls for exactly this reason. The statement shows both debits, and the duplicate debit sits open against the nostro until the duplicate funds come back.


#### Mirror-account drift from unadvised fees and interest


Unadvised charges, interest, and other missing entries all create the same mirror-account drift when the internal posting is absent.


A lack of visibility on available funds leads to overfunding, and aging breaks can hide worse problems. Fraud or a correspondent's operational error can sit in the mirror-versus-statement gap for days before anyone notices.


The generic exception workflow for aging breaks is in[high-volume reconciliation patterns](https://www.formance.com/blog/financial-operations/account-reconciliation-patterns-for-high-volume-fintech) for fintechs.


### How a core ledger reconciles nostro accounts against correspondent statements


A core ledger closes the nostro-vs-statement gap by combining two things: a data model that separates instructed from settled movements, and an ingestion contract that keeps that model in sync with statement data.


Formance is an open-source,[programmable core ledger](https://www.formance.com/modules/ledger) that unifies fiat and digital assets with regulatory-grade traceability. It sits alongside your existing core banking system, and implements the mirror-plus-in-transit model as ordinary accounts, runs as a single atomic Numscript transaction, and enforces the four ingestion rules.


#### Model the nostro as a mirror plus an in-transit account


The nostro is a pair of accounts: a mirror for the expected position after instructed movements, and an in-transit account for instructed-but-unconfirmed movements.


The statement balance stays as the separately observed, confirmed external position. An outbound instruction moves funds from the mirror to in-transit. The statement line that confirms the movement moves funds from in-transit to the external world.


An expected inbound credit runs from the external world into in-transit when the advice arrives, then from in-transit to the mirror when the statement confirms the credit.


Every statement line posts against the mirror and in-transit accounts. The statement's identifiers travel with the posting as metadata, so you can always trace a break back to the statement line that caused it.


#### Reconciling a $2.5M inbound credit in Numscript


An expected inward credit of $2,500,000 from a counterparty at correspondent A arrives on the camt.053 as $2,250,000, which is a $250,000 shortfall against the mirror posting.


Four account paths are involved:


1


@nostro:corr_a:usd:mirror


2


@nostro:corr_a:usd:in_transit


3


@fees:corr_a:lifting


4


@recon:corr_a:usd:unexplained


When the counterparty told you the payment was coming, the $2,500,000 was posted to in-transit.


The camt.053 statement line clears the in-transit balance. $2,250,000 moves from in-transit to the mirror as principal, and the $250,000 shortfall moves from in-transit to @recon:corr_a:usd:unexplained with the statement identifiers attached. In-transit returns to zero, and the mirror equals the statement balance.


The transaction carries statement_id, entry_ref, value_date, and booking_date as metadata, with value date and booking date kept separate.


[Numscript](https://www.formance.com/platform/numscript) , Formance's purpose-built language for money that describes transaction intent in terms both engineers and finance teams can read, writes the principal leg and the exception leg as one atomic transaction with two posting legs.


A partial write cannot leave the in-transit account half-cleared.


```text
// NOSTRO_STATEMENT_RECONCILIATION
// Event: clear an inbound payment against the statement and route the shortfall to the exception account


send   [USD/2 225000000]   (
source   =   @nostro:corr_a:usd:in_transit
destination   =   @nostro:corr_a:usd:mirror
)


send   [USD/2 25000000]   (
source   =   @nostro:corr_a:usd:in_transit
destination   =   @recon:corr_a:usd:unexplained
)


set_tx_meta  (  "event_type"  ,   "nostro_statement_reconciliation"  )
set_tx_meta  (  "statement_id"  ,   "camt053-corr_a-usd-2026-09-15"  )
set_tx_meta  (  "entry_ref"  ,   "ENTRY-4471"  )
set_tx_meta  (  "value_date"  ,   "2026-09-15"  )
set_tx_meta  (  "booking_date"  ,   "2026-09-16"  )


```


#### Statement ingestion contract: idempotent, bi-temporal, and continuous


Statement ingestion must be idempotent, bi-temporal, and continuous. Otherwise, the mirror-plus-in-transit model drifts within a week.


Four rules keep it stable:


1


**Key every ingested line on statement ID plus entry reference** , so a resent file posts nothing new.


2


**Record both the booking date and the ingestion date** , so a corrected line lands on the right effective date without rewriting history. The query side uses[temporal query execution](https://www.formance.com/blog/engineering/execution-of-temporal-queries-on-third-party-data) .


3


**Send every unexplained residual to an exception account** instead of forcing a match. Old outstanding items signal a settlement error.


4


**Normalize correspondent events at one boundary** , so MT940 and camt.053 entries post with the same shape, following a[multi-rail architecture](https://www.formance.com/blog/engineering/money-movement-architecture-for-multi-rail-fintechs) .
